items.context: The GCT review flags files >500 lines. We have 46 Go files and 24 TS/TSX files exceeding this. Some files are slightly over (500-600 lines) and splitting them may create unnecessary churn. We need to decide where to draw the line for mandatory splitting vs. leaving alone.

options.label: Split everything over 500 lines (match GCT threshold exactly)
options.rationale: Maximizes violation count reduction. Every split directly reduces the long_files count. But some 500-600 line files may not benefit structurally from splitting.

options.label: Split files over 700 lines, leave 500-700 for opportunistic cleanup
options.rationale: Focuses effort on the worst offenders (30+ Go files, 10+ TS/TSX files above 700). The 500-700 range files may naturally shrink when complex functions are extracted in Phase 3. Recommended because it maximizes impact per effort and avoids unnecessary churn on borderline files.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own threshold or approach

items.context: The largest frontend files are GeneratorForm.tsx (979 lines), pipelineStore.ts (878 lines), SigningPage.tsx (687 lines), and PreflightSection.tsx (624 lines). These are structurally different: GeneratorForm is a monolithic form, pipelineStore is a Zustand store with polling logic, SigningPage and PreflightSection are page-level components with multiple sections.

options.label: Extract sub-components and custom hooks
options.rationale: Split GeneratorForm into section sub-components (e.g., GeneratorFormHeader, GeneratorFormConfig, GeneratorFormActions). Extract polling/rate-limiting logic from pipelineStore into separate utility hooks. Recommended because it follows React best practices and reduces both line count and complexity.

options.label: Extract only custom hooks, keep components intact
options.rationale: Move reusable logic into hooks but keep component structure unchanged. Less disruptive but may not bring files below threshold.

items.context: 100 complex_functions violations exist, concentrated in orchestrator.go (28 functions), service.go files, and handler files. Common complexity patterns in this codebase: deeply nested switch/case in state machines, multi-step error handling chains, and large conditional blocks in pipeline stages.

options.label: Early returns + guard clauses first, then extract helpers
options.rationale: Flatten nesting with early returns as the primary technique, then extract remaining complex blocks into named helper functions. Recommended because early returns are the lowest-risk refactor (no new functions to wire up) and often sufficient alone to drop cyclomatic complexity below threshold.

options.label: Extract helper functions first, then simplify remaining logic
options.rationale: Pull out cohesive blocks into well-named helpers, reducing each function's line count and complexity. More structural change but creates better-named abstractions.

options.label: Table-driven refactoring for switch/case heavy functions
options.rationale: Replace large switch statements with map lookups or table-driven dispatch. Effective for state machines but may reduce readability for unfamiliar maintainers.

items.context: This is the 3rd largest Go file and lives in the cli/ directory, not api/. It contains CLI command definitions for the pipeline. The acceptance_allow pattern covers scenarios/scenario-to-desktop/** which includes cli/. This file was not called out in the plan's key offenders table.

options.label: Split by command group (e.g., commands_run.go, commands_status.go, commands_config.go)
options.rationale: CLI commands naturally group by subcommand. Splitting by group keeps related code together and is a clean structural decomposition. Recommended because CLI command files are the easiest to split — each command is self-contained.

options.label: Defer to Phase 2 but deprioritize vs. api/ files
options.rationale: Focus effort on api/ and runtime/ first since they have more violations. Address cli/ only if time permits.

items.text: The validation report flagged two missing items in plan.md: (1) no greenfield declaration — since this is pure refactoring with no backward compatibility concerns, a greenfield declaration is appropriate, and (2) no `vrooli scenario restart` final cleanup step in the rollout checklist. Both will be added to the updated plan.
